Browser Support Matrix#

Customer-readable. Which browsers get which experience, decided by web/playground/caps.js at page load and reported in the status line.

A scene link opens in any current browser. Browsers with WebGPU — Chrome, Edge, Safari 26, Firefox on Windows and macOS — get the full picture. Everything else that has WebGL2 (older iPhones and iPads, Firefox on Linux and Android, most in-app browsers) gets a lighter build that streams the same scene the same way, with walk, tour, review pins, measuring and video export. It also gets the same studio lighting, shadows, contact shadow, bloom, ambient occlusion, per-room reflections, real-time GI and uploaded HDR backgrounds as WebGPU — measured within mean ΔE76 0.3 of the WebGPU picture on products. Still WebGPU-only: path-traced stills, screen-space reflections, the scene-wide mirror probe, temporal upscaling and HDR display output. Gaussian-splat captures need WebGPU.

Every page load lands in one of four tiers, chosen from what the browser actually exposes — not from a user-agent guess — and the tier is telemetered so we know what real traffic gets.

Tiers#

TierRequirementsWhat renders
AWebGPU adapter with desktop-class limits, OffscreenCanvasFull pipeline: streamed virtualized geometry (scenes far larger than device memory), clustered lights, SSAO, bloom, temporal super-resolution ("4K mode"), HDR environments, mirror probes, glass, GPU picking, WebXR.
BWebGPU adapter with mobile-class limits, OffscreenCanvasSame pipeline with reduced budgets: smaller streaming pool, dynamic resolution scaling, thermal governor steps quality down before the device throttles.
CNo WebGPU; WebGL2 availableClassic GLB scenes AND streamed scenes. A shared streamed link opens with the same streaming as tier A/B: the level-of-detail cut is selected on the CPU, geometry and textures stream on demand into device-sized pools (phone class: 1K texture slots; desktop class: 2K slots and 4× MSAA), with sun shadows, picking, walk, tour, review and video export. Since 4.0: studio environment lighting, contact shadow, bloom, optional SSAO, 4× MSAA on desktop class, per-room reflection probes (phones at half resolution) and real-time GI; a frame-time governor steps bloom / AO / MSAA / shadow resolution down on a hot phone. No SSR, no ray-traced reflections, no TSR, no path-traced stills, no splats.
–NeitherPoster image (if the page supplied one), a one-line explanation, and — only inside an in-app WebView — a "open in your browser" link.

Two further capabilities shape the experience within a tier:

  • Cross-origin isolation (SharedArrayBuffer): our origin sends the COOP/COEP headers, so on our pages the simulation runs in its own worker and publishes through a lock-free triple buffer. Where isolation is unavailable, the render worker runs a camera-only world — same visuals, slightly less input smoothness under load. Partner pages embedding via embed.js never need these headers: the engine runs in an iframe served from our origin.
  • Compressed texture formats: the decode worker transcodes KTX2/Basis to whatever the device supports (BC7 / ASTC / ETC2, else RGBA8). Memory use, not visuals, is what changes.

Browsers#

BrowserWebGPUTypical tierNotes
Chrome / Edge 113+ on Windows, macOS, ChromeOSyesAReference platform: our automated suites run in Chromium on macOS, and have run on Windows on Intel Arc and NVIDIA (below).
Chrome 121+ on Android 12+yes (ARM, Qualcomm and Intel GPUs; Imagination GPUs from Chrome 139 on Android 16)B; C on Qualcomm Adreno without timestamp queriesLimits and thermals drive the reduced budgets. Qualcomm Adreno phones (e.g. Galaxy S23, Z Flip5) open on WebGPU when the adapter offers timestamp-query — the engine then fences every render pass, which on a real Galaxy S23 (Adreno 740, Chrome 149) kept textured scenes at 30 fps with no device loss (7 of 8 runs, October 2026); without it they open on the WebGL2 build. An early device loss still falls back to WebGL2 (below). ?tier=c / ?tier=a force either build.
Samsung Internet 24+yesB; C on Qualcomm Adreno without timestamp queriesFollows Chrome on Android.
Safari 26 on macOS 26 (Tahoe)yesA/BLimits vary by machine. Safari 18 and earlier: tier C.
Safari — and every other browser — on iOS / iPadOS 26yesA/B (phone budget)All iOS browsers use Safari's engine, so Chrome on an iPhone behaves the same. Since 19 Oct 2026 iPhones and iPads open on WebGPU with a phone-class memory budget (the early-October crash was tier A's desktop-sized pools, charged by WebKit to the tab); ?tier=c pins the WebGL2 build, and a device whose WebGPU device dies early falls back to it and is remembered. iOS 17 and 18: tier C. iOS 16 and earlier (Safari before 17 cannot draw WebGL on an OffscreenCanvas): the viewer says "Update your iPhone or iPad to iOS 17 or later" instead of loading.

WebGPU availability as of 2 October 2026, from caniuse.com/webgpu and the WebGPU working group's implementation status page. The two disagree on Firefox (caniuse lists it as off by default); the row above follows the working group's page.

What we have run ourselves: Chromium on macOS, on every release, with both builds; Chromium on Windows 11 on an Intel Arc and an NVIDIA GPU (October 2026, below). Real phones (October 2026, BrowserStack): iPhone 15 on iOS 17 and iOS 26, iPhone 13 on iOS 16.3 (update message, by design), iPad Air 13 on iOS 18, Galaxy M32 (Android 11) — all Safari/Chrome, tier C on Apple devices; Galaxy S23 Chrome (Adreno 740: WebGPU lost its device until the pass-fence fix; with it WebGPU renders, and the WebGL2 build renders too) and Pixel 8 Chrome (Mali-G715: WebGPU renders). Other phone rows follow the browsers' published WebGPU status; no headset has been verified.

A WebGPU device that is lost within the first minute of a session (or twice in one session) reloads the page into the WebGL2 build, and that browser's GPU is remembered for two weeks so later visits open on WebGL2 directly.

Verified on Windows#

One laptop, both of its GPUs: Windows 11 (26200), Intel Core Ultra 7 356H, headless Chromium 151 (Playwright's full build), WebGPU on Dawn / D3D12 and WebGL2 on ANGLE / D3D11. The adapter was confirmed per run from navigator.gpu.requestAdapter().info and WebGL's UNMASKED_RENDERER (web/test/tools/gpu-probe.mjs); Chrome 155 and Edge 155 were confirmed to create a WebGPU device on both GPUs, but the gates ran on Chromium.

PlatformTier A (WebGPU / D3D12)Tier C (WebGL2 / ANGLE D3D11)Verified (16 October 2026)
Windows 11 + Intel Arc (Intel Graphics 0xB0A0, Xe3-LPG — the Core Ultra 7 356H's integrated GPU)✓✓materials: 88 / 89 — the one miss, IridescentDishWithOlives tier C desktop (ΔE 6.04 vs 6), is known, fails on macOS too, fixed in 4.0
Windows 11 + NVIDIA (GeForce RTX 5060 Laptop GPU, Blackwell)✓✓materials: 88 / 89 — the one miss, IridescentDishWithOlives tier C desktop (ΔE 6.05 vs 6), is known, fails on macOS too, fixed in 4.0

Compressed textures on both: BC7 (texture-compression-bc; Windows GPUs expose no ASTC / ETC2, so those transcode legs are skipped, not failed). Not covered on this machine: the private test scenes (a shoe scan, a villa, an archviz flat) and the old structure compile (private fixtures — every leg that needs them reported skipped), Firefox, and a visible (non-headless) window. Known open item: in 1 of 7 appshell runs on the Intel GPU, Chrome lost the GPU for the rest of the browser session ("Graphics stopped in this browser"); not reproduced in the 4 runs since (3 with GPU-process logging), and no driver reset in the Windows event log.

Tier is decided per session at load; the same browser can land in A or B depending on the adapter's reported limits.

In-app WebViews#

Most direct-to-consumer links open inside an app, not a browser. These WebViews frequently lack WebGPU, sometimes lack SharedArrayBuffer, and throttle aggressively. The engine detects them and reports the app name in telemetry (inApp), so a downgrade is visible rather than silent.

WebViewDetected asWhat usually happens
InstagraminstagramTier C on most devices (the WebGL2 build streams the scene); poster + "open in your browser" when WebGL2 is missing.
Facebook / MessengerfacebookSame as Instagram.
WhatsAppwhatsappSame.
TikToktiktokSame; the most aggressive throttling seen.
Pinterest, Snapchat, LINE, X/Twitterpinterest, snapchat, line, twitterSame.

Only inside a WebView does the fallback offer "open in your browser" — that is the one situation where it is genuinely the fix, and the engine avoids nagging real browsers with it.

Colour output is decided per session and reported in window.__verseColor ({ p3, p3Display, requested, hdr }). Auto = the page's own media queries: (color-gamut: p3) → Display-P3 canvas, (dynamic-range: high) → HDR canvas (tier A only). A browser that ignores the request keeps the sRGB canvas and the shaders encode for what it actually got, so a wrong guess can never over-saturate. Golden captures pin sRGB.

Engine download (brotli): 522 KB for the WebGPU build, 449 KB for the WebGL2 build (raw WebGL2, no wgpu, build-time-translated GLSL); the JPEG / WebP / HDR codec module is fetched only when the engine has to decode one of those.

Reasons in the status line#

When a session lands below tier A, caps.reasons lists why — these are the strings you will see in telemetry and in the fallback panel:

no-offscreencanvas · not-cross-origin-isolated · no-navigator-gpu · no-webgpu-adapter · webgpu-request-failed · no-webgl2 · ios-webgl-default (iPhone / iPad, only while caps.js IOS_WEBGPU_DEFAULT is off) · android-adreno-no-timestamps (an Adreno phone without timestamp queries) · webgpu-remembered-bad (this browser's GPU lost its WebGPU device recently).

Testing#

  • web/test/qa-suite.mjs includes tier-C forcing (?tier=c); splats are refused there with a message.
  • web/test/fix-verify-tierc-stream.mjs opens each streamed scene on both builds with the same camera and compares the pictures.
  • web/test/fix-verify-claims.mjs keeps this page, the product page and the upload screen in step with the engine: what this page says a browser without WebGPU gets must match STREAMED_SCENES_NEED_WEBGPU in web/playground/caps.js, which must match the WebGL2 renderer.
  • web/test/golden.mjs renders both builds headlessly and compares to committed goldens per platform (GOLDEN_PLATFORM=darwin diffs another machine against the Mac set; GOLDEN_NO_APPROVE=1 fails on a missing golden instead of approving the current render).
  • On a multi-GPU machine, node --import ./tools/gpu-select.mjs <gate> (run from web/test) with VERSE_GPU=nvidia|intel (high-performance / low-power) pins every gate's Chromium to one adapter; on Windows it also uses the full Chromium build, because the default chrome-headless-shell cannot create a WebGPU device there (no DXC DLLs).
  • Physical-device rows on the metrics wall (docs/metrics-wall.md) are emulated until the launch hardware is in hand — treat the mobile tiers above as verified in emulation, not on-device.
